paras: The threatened lynching of Sherman Stevens took place in Randolph County, Alabama, in the summer of 1903, when a crowd planned to take Stevens, a Black prisoner accused of killing his father, from the jail at Wedowee. Sheriff Kent and a deputy moved him to Opelika before the crowd assembled, and the Montgomery Advertiser headed its report "Lynching Prevented." Open lynching threats were made again at his trial in August, and he was convicted, sentenced to death and legally hanged at Wedowee in September.

According to a Wedowee dispatch, Stevens, described as "colored," shot and mortally wounded his father, Lee Stevens, during a disturbance at a protracted meeting at a Black church just west of town the previous October. A later report placed the killing in November and at a "negro camp meeting." Stevens eluded officers for nearly a year until A. L. Kent and Z. T. McMurray captured him about eight miles south of Wedowee, and he was jailed on Saturday, June 20, 1903.

By then the paper's correspondent said he was "thought to be" the man who had criminally assaulted a Mrs. Kelly about two weeks earlier, some fifteen miles northeast of Wedowee. The state had offered a $100 reward for his arrest on the murder charge, and citizens of the community promised another if he was shown guilty of the assault.

On July 1, word reached Wedowee that on Monday evening about 100 persons from Cleburne County had gathered at an iron bridge five miles from town. They were to meet a crowd from near Graham, where Mrs. Kelly was said to have been assaulted, and then go to the jail to "secure the person" of Stevens. Sheriff Kent and Deputy Fuller carried Stevens to Opelika that night for safekeeping, and the Graham crowd never appeared.

A Roanoke correspondent later gave a compressed account, saying a mob was organized to lynch Stevens "when he was captured" and that the officers took him on the early train to Opelika, where he remained until the trial.

Stevens was returned to Wedowee and tried on the murder charge on August 21 before one of the largest crowds ever seen in the town. The Advertiser's correspondent wrote that "there were open threats that the negro would be lynched if the jury failed to affix the death penalty." The jury agreed on a guilty verdict in a few minutes, and when many spectators applauded, Judge Denson rebuked them.

Stevens was hanged at Wedowee on September 25, 1903, before an estimated 3,000 people from Randolph and adjoining counties. Sheriff Kent made the execution public except for screening the body after the drop, and the report called it the second legal hanging in the county's history. No charge against Stevens for the assault on Mrs. Kelly and no arrests of the crowd appear in the coverage.

Every detailed account came from the Montgomery Advertiser, which printed special dispatches from Wedowee and Roanoke at each stage, from the arrest in June to the hanging in September. Its July report praised the sheriff and his deputy for protecting their prisoner but remarked that, since the Graham crowd failed to show up, there was no "party." The August trial report, headed "Notorious Parricide is Given the Death Sentence," recorded the lynching threats without comment and said circumstances pointed to Stevens "as the guilty wretch" in the assault case, although he was never tried for it.

The only Black-press notice found was a single line in the Richmond Planet's weekly news digest, reporting that Stevens had been hanged at Wedowee for the murder of his father. That item misplaced Wedowee in Virginia and made no mention of the mob or the threats at trial.

The reports differ on the spelling of his name, Sherman in the June and July dispatches and in the Planet but Sharman in the August and September ones. They also differ on timing: the July dispatch placed the gathering about ten days after his capture, while the August report said the mob formed at the time of capture, and the earlier, contemporaneous account is the more specific.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Sherman Stevens
bases: A crowd gathered to take Stevens from the Wedowee jail and was forestalled when officers moved him to Opelika (A2, A3), and open lynching threats were made at his trial (A3); the threatened lynching is the episode, and his later death was a court-ordered hanging (A4).

A crowd of about 100 planned to take Stevens from jail over an alleged assault (A2) and threats were repeated at his trial (A3), but no mob killed him (killed and illegal refer to his death); he died by a legal execution after conviction in circuit court (A4, A5).

The mob threats appear only in the Montgomery Advertiser, in two separate dispatches (A2, A3); the arrest, conviction and hanging are reported by the Advertiser (A1, A3, A4) and the hanging alone by the Richmond Planet's digest (A5).
